results.claim: For m,n≥2, the sortable component has Q=(mn)! states if m or n is even and Q=(mn)!/2 states if both are odd.
results.proof_sketch: A row push is an n-cycle and a column push is an m-cycle. Thus when m and n are odd every generator is even, so only even configurations are reachable. The sortable-instance characterization in the sealed source gives the converse and also says that if either dimension is even every permutation is reachable. Hence the component of the sorted state has exactly the stated size.

results.claim: On a p×q board where pushes in both directions are allowed, an involution π on any chosen row can be applied in at most 3q+3a₂(π) pushes, with the only side effect being a one-step cyclic shift, in a chosen direction, of the body of each of a₂(π) fixed auxiliary columns.
results.proof_sketch: Use the source's three-scan SwapPairs construction, assigning one distinct auxiliary column to each transposition. In its one-direction model, a required inverse column push is represented by p−1 forward pushes. In the bidirectional target model, replace that block by one opposite-direction push, which is exactly the same permutation. Each scan makes q row pushes and one push of every auxiliary column, hence 3q+3a₂(π) pushes. The source's position trace is unchanged: the requested pairs swap, every other chosen-row token stays fixed, each auxiliary-column body shifts by one, and all other positions remain fixed.

results.claim: Every even permutation is a product συ of two involutions with a₂(σ)=a₂(υ); every odd permutation is a product συτ where τ is a transposition and a₂(σ)=a₂(υ).
results.proof_sketch: Factor each cycle into two reflections. An odd-length cycle has factors containing equally many transpositions. An even-length cycle has two choices whose transposition counts differ by +1 or −1. An even permutation has an even number of even-length cycles, so alternate the two choices to balance the totals. For an odd permutation, leave one unit of imbalance and remove one transposition τ from the larger final involution. Combining the disjoint factors gives the stated products.

results.claim: For adjacent rows r,r+1 and adjacent columns c,c+1, the eight-push word R_r^{-1}C_c^{-1}R_rC_cC_{c+1}R_{r+1}C_{c+1}^{-1}R_{r+1}^{-1} swaps the two positions in columns c,c+1 in each of those two rows and fixes every other position; its transpose gives the analogous pair of vertical swaps.
results.proof_sketch: Directly track the four intersections through the word; the two horizontal pairs are exchanged and every other cell returns. Consequently, for any even subset S of k parallel lines, the same fixed adjacent transposition can be applied exactly on precisely the lines in S using at most 8(k−1) pushes. Regard the lines as vertices of a path and select edge i exactly when |S∩{1,…,i}| is odd. The selected adjacent-line double swaps give odd incidence exactly at S, and the target transpositions commute.

results.claim: On any m×n board with m,n≥2, every globally even permutation that preserves each row setwise, or preserves each column setwise, can be performed exactly in O(mn) bidirectional pushes.
results.proof_sketch: Consider k parallel lines of length ℓ, so kℓ=mn. On each line whose desired permutation is even, the balanced-involution factorization and two opposite-direction involution calls realize it exactly in at most 9ℓ pushes, with all side effects cancelled. For an odd line permutation π, fix the same adjacent transposition t on every line and write π=(πt)t; πt is even. Since the whole layer is even, the number of odd lines is even. The preceding path construction realizes the product T of all residual copies of t in O(k) pushes. If E is the product of the independently realizable even factors, then the desired layer is ET, so perform T and then E. The total is O(kℓ+k)=O(mn). Transposition gives the column version.

results.claim: Every permutation P of the mn cells admits a three-layer factorization P=C₂RC₁, where C₁ and C₂ preserve every column setwise and R preserves every row setwise.
results.proof_sketch: Make a bipartite multigraph whose left and right vertices are respectively source and destination columns, with one edge for each token. Every vertex has degree m. For X on the left, the m|X| incident edges enter N(X), which can receive at most m|N(X)| edges, so Hall's condition holds. Remove a perfect matching and repeat; this colors the edges with m perfect matchings. Use colors as intermediate rows. C₁ puts each token into its matching-color row within its source column. In each color row, the matching uses every destination column once, so R sends every token to its destination column. C₂ then sends it to its destination row. This proves the factorization.

results.claim: Every even permutation of an m×n board with m,n≥2 is realizable in O(mn) bidirectional pushes.
results.proof_sketch: Take P=L₃L₂L₁ from the column-row-column factorization. Because P is even, zero or two of the layers are odd. For each odd L_i choose a transposition τ_i within one of its lines and put E_i=L_iτ_i; for an even layer put τ_i=1 and E_i=L_i. All E_i are even line-preserving layers, hence cost O(mn) each by the preceding claim. With E=E₃E₂E₁, expansion gives E^{-1}P=(E₁^{-1}E₂^{-1}τ₃E₂E₁)(E₁^{-1}τ₂E₁)τ₁. Thus K=E^{-1}P is a product of zero or two transpositions. It is therefore the identity, one 3-cycle, or two disjoint transpositions. The latter is a product of two 3-cycles. The sealed source's arbitrary three-token cycle uses a constant number of compound rotations, hence O(max{m,n})=O(mn) bidirectional unit pushes. Since P=EK, the total is O(mn).

results.claim: Every sortable m×n configuration with m,n≥2 can be sorted in O(mn) bidirectional pushes.
results.proof_sketch: If the configuration permutation is even, apply the preceding construction to its inverse. If it is odd, sortability implies that at least one dimension is even. A unit rotation of a line of that even length is an odd permutation g. Multiplying the desired odd permutation by g^{-1} leaves an even permutation, which costs O(mn), and the remaining g costs one push. On an odd-by-odd board every sortable permutation is even, so these cases exhaust all sortable configurations.

results.claim: If min{m,n}=1 and N=mn, then D(m,n)=floor(N/2).
results.proof_sketch: Only the unique nontrivial row or column can move, so its reachable configurations are precisely its N cyclic shifts. A shift by a positions has distance d_N(a)=min(a mod N,N−(a mod N)); maximizing over a gives floor(N/2). This also covers N=1, where the diameter is zero.

results.claim: Every instance A has the displacement certificate pn(A)≥ceil(H(A)/n)+ceil(V(A)/m). Moreover, a global translation by a columns and b rows has exact push number m·d_n(a)+n·d_m(b), where d_k(z)=min(z mod k,k−(z mod k)).
results.proof_sketch: A row push changes the total cyclic horizontal displacement H by at most n and leaves V unchanged, so any sorting word contains at least ceil(H/n) row pushes. Symmetrically it contains at least ceil(V/m) column pushes, and the counts add. For a global translation, H=mn·d_n(a) and V=mn·d_m(b). Rotating every row and column back along shortest directions attains the resulting lower bound.

results.claim: The maximum possible value of the displacement certificate is exactly m·floor(n/2)+n·floor(m/2), which is at most N=mn; a half-translation attains it.
results.proof_sketch: Each token contributes at most floor(n/2) to H and floor(m/2) to V. Hence H≤N floor(n/2) and V≤N floor(m/2), so ceil(H/n)+ceil(V/m)≤m floor(n/2)+n floor(m/2)≤N. Translating every token by floor(n/2) columns and floor(m/2) rows makes every token attain both maxima simultaneously. Thus the bound and the claimed exact translation distance are attained.

results.claim: For arbitrary p,q≥2, FillColumns makes every column near-full using O(pq log q) pushes; the proof does not require p≤q.
results.proof_sketch: Each column is pushed at most p−1 times. Let Ψ count tokens lying in the body of a column other than their target column, and let f be the number of underfull columns. The conveyor argument shows that every complete block of q buffer-row pushes decreases Ψ by at least f/2. During a phase with q/2^i≤f<q/2^{i−1}, one has Ψ<(p−1)q/2^{i−1}, so fewer than 4p complete blocks occur. There are O(log q) phases, giving O(pq log q) row pushes, while all column pushes total O(pq). No inequality compares p with q.

results.claim: For arbitrary p,q≥2, FloatMinimums transforms a matrix whose columns are all near-full into one whose columns are all body-full using O(pq) pushes.
results.proof_sketch: Near-fullness implies that the buffer row contains exactly one token for each target column. During one q-step sweep, each such token aligns with its target column. Rotate that column by at most p−1 steps until its unique target-buffer token is at the head, and never rotate it again during this procedure. Its body then contains exactly the p−1 nonbuffer tokens assigned to that column. The total is q+q(p−1)=pq.

results.claim: Given a p×q matrix in which every column is body-full, its buffer row can be sorted in O(q) bidirectional pushes while preserving the set of tokens in every column body.
results.proof_sketch: The heads are exactly the q buffer tokens. If their required permutation is even, factor it into two equal-size involutions and apply the bidirectional involution construction with opposite side-effect directions on the same auxiliary columns; every body shift cancels. If it is odd, use the corresponding factorization with one final transposition. That last call shifts one body cyclically but preserves its token set. Since every involution has at most q/2 transpositions, the total cost is O(q).

results.claim: For arbitrary m,n≥2 and N=mn, any m×n configuration can be transformed in O(N log m) pushes into one in which every row contains exactly its target-row token set. In particular, this costs O(N log min{m,n}) when m≤n.
results.proof_sketch: Transpose the board and relabel each target (r,c) as (c,r), obtaining dimensions p=n and q=m. Apply the dimension-independent FillColumns bound in O(pq log q), FloatMinimums in O(pq), and buffer-head cleanup in O(q). Every transposed column then contains its complete target-column token set. Transposing the description back gives correct target-row membership in the original board. Since pq=N and q=m, the cost is O(N log m). This proof is valid for tall boards too, but then its logarithm is log m, not log min{m,n}.

results.claim: The parent's short-dimension reorientation does not justify its former row-specific O(N log min{m,n}) conclusion on a fixed tall labeling.
results.proof_sketch: For the audited 3×2 input ((1,2),(3,5),(4,6)), that construction can output ((1,2),(5,4),(3,6)). The output columns are {1,3,5} and {2,4,6}, exactly their target-column sets, but its second and third rows are {4,5} and {3,6}, not the target-row sets {3,4} and {5,6}. Conceptually, orienting a tall board with its short dimension as rows exchanges the two coordinate objectives: oriented-row membership maps back to original-column membership. Thus that transpose-back inference is invalid.

results.claim: Assume 2≤m≤n and every row of a sortable m×n board already contains exactly its target-row token set. The board can then be sorted in O(mn) bidirectional pushes.
results.proof_sketch: An even row correction is a product of two equal-size involutions; opposite-direction calls realize it in O(n) and cancel every off-row change. If a correction is odd and n is even, one row push makes the residual even. If n is odd and m is even, realize the even part and one transposition; the resulting cycle on an auxiliary column's m−1-cell body is even and can be reversed by two transposed involution calls in O(m). If both dimensions are odd, global sortability makes the number of odd row corrections even. Reduce each such row to the same adjacent transposition and use adjacent double swaps to repair them. The total is O(mn).

results.claim: Let D(m,n) be the maximum push number of a sortable m×n instance, N=mn, and s=min{m,n}. The earlier constructive route gives D(m,n)=O(N·max{1,log s}), and in particular O(N log s) for m,n≥2.
results.proof_sketch: For s≥2, orient the entire sorting problem as an s×t board with t=max{m,n}. Apply the row-membership construction with m=s, obtaining correct target-row sets in O(N log s), and then the row-sorting result in O(N). This use of transposition is legitimate because the entire sorting objective, unlike a row-specific intermediate conclusion on a fixed labeling, is coordinate-invariant. The one-dimensional result handles s=1. The structural construction above strengthens this upper bound to O(N).

results.claim: For all m,n≥2, every configuration, including a nonsortable odd configuration on an odd-by-odd board, can be transformed in O(mn) pushes into one with correct target-row token sets.
results.proof_sketch: If either dimension is even, every configuration is sortable and the linear diameter construction sorts it. If both are odd, an even configuration likewise sorts. For an odd configuration A, let B be the sorted board with two tokens in one row transposed. Then B is odd and has correct row sets. The relative permutation from A to B is even, so the linear construction moves A to B in O(mn). This is a corollary of the new diameter proof and is independent of the invalid short-dimension transpose-back inference.

results.claim: For every fixed s≥2, boards with min{m,n}=s have asymptotically tight push number D(m,n)=Θ(mn).
results.proof_sketch: This follows already from the earlier O(N log s)=O(N) bound for fixed s and the half-translation lower bound m·floor(n/2)+n·floor(m/2)=Ω(N). It is also an immediate special case of the new uniform Θ(N) theorem.

results.claim: For m,n≥2, a counting lower bound is D(m,n)≥ceil(log_{d−1}(1+(d−2)(Q−1)/d)), where d=2(m+n), Q=(mn)! if m or n is even, and Q=(mn)!/2 otherwise.
results.proof_sketch: There are Q sortable configurations. A geodesic word never immediately follows a generator with its inverse, so words of length at most L have at most 1+d((d−1)^L−1)/(d−2) possible endpoints. Coincident generators on two-cell lines only make this an overcount. The radius-D ball must contain all Q states; rearranging gives the displayed ceiling. The restriction m,n≥2 is essential: on a 1×9 board the component has 9 states and D=4, whereas substituting 9!/2 in the former overbroad claim falsely gave 5.

results.claim: For m,n≥2, the numerical counting certificate above is always at most 2N, so this reduced-word obstruction cannot establish a superlinear lower bound.
results.proof_sketch: Put X=1+(d−2)(Q−1)/d. Since Q>1, X<Q≤N!<N^N. Also d−1=2(m+n)−1>sqrt(N), using m+n≥2sqrt(N). Therefore log_{d−1}X<N log_{d−1}N<2N. Since 2N is an integer, ceil(log_{d−1}X)≤2N.

results.claim: Global translations are not generally diametral: D(2,3)=7, whereas every translated 2×3 board has distance at most 5.
results.proof_sketch: Exact breadth-first search reported in the sealed audit uses the seven distinct 2×3 generators and visits all 720 configurations with level sizes [1,7,31,115,274,253,36,3], so the diameter is 7. The seven-push word R1-left, C1-up, R1-left, C1-up, C3-up, R1-right, C1-up reaches ((3,2,1),(6,5,4)), whose exact distance is 7. The displacement formula gives maximum translation distance 2·floor(3/2)+3·floor(2/2)=5.

results.claim: Exact square boundary cases give D(2,2)=4 and D(3,3)=8; on 3×3 the maximum displacement certificate is 6 and the corrected two-dimensional counting certificate is 5.
results.proof_sketch: The sealed audit's complete BFS gives level sizes [1,4,10,8,1] on the 24-state 2×2 component and [1,12,96,736,5208,28674,89497,54741,2475] on the 181440-state 3×3 component. Thus their last nonempty levels are 4 and 8. The exact displacement maximum formula gives 4 and 6, while the reduced-word formula gives 2 and 5. These examples show that the two lower-bound certificates need not be tight, although the structural upper bound makes that limitation irrelevant to asymptotic target coverage.

results.claim: Let N=mn. Uniformly for m,n≥2, D(m,n)=Θ(N); together with D(1,N)=D(N,1)=floor(N/2), this closes the source's multiplicative logarithmic gap at the requested asymptotic strength.
results.proof_sketch: The structural column-row-column construction gives D(m,n)=O(N). For the reverse inequality, take the half-translation. Its exact distance is m·floor(n/2)+n·floor(m/2). Since floor(k/2)≥k/3 for every integer k≥2, this is at least 2N/3, so D(m,n)=Ω(N) uniformly. In one dimension the exact cyclic diameter is floor(N/2). Hence the worst-case push number is linear, with no remaining regime in which a logarithmic factor is unresolved.

final_writeup:
The structural-reformulation lens closes the gap. Write N=mn and first assume m,n≥2. The key intermediate object is not a partially sorted board but a three-layer routing of the desired position permutation. Build an m-regular bipartite multigraph between source columns and destination columns, one edge per token. Hall's theorem gives a perfect matching; deleting it and repeating decomposes the graph into m perfect matchings. Treat their colors as intermediate rows. A first column-local permutation puts each token in its color row, a row-local permutation sends it to its destination column, and a final column-local permutation sends it to its destination row. Thus every desired permutation factors as C₂RC₁.

It remains to realize the layers cheaply despite parity. First consider any row- or column-preserving layer that is globally even. An even permutation on one line factors into two involutions with equal numbers of transpositions. The audited bidirectional SwapPairs construction applies each involution in O(line length) pushes, and opposite body-shift directions cancel, so the line permutation is exact. For every odd local permutation, split off the same fixed adjacent transposition. A globally even layer has an even number of such residual transpositions. The exact eight-push double-swap word applies that transposition on two adjacent parallel lines. On the path of lines, choosing edge i when the prefix contains an odd number of residual lines realizes every residual simultaneously with at most one double swap per path edge. Hence every globally even line-preserving layer costs O(N).

Now let an even target permutation have routing layers L₃L₂L₁. Their parities contain zero or two odd layers. For each odd layer choose a line-supported transposition τ_i and set E_i=L_iτ_i; all E_i are even layers and therefore cost O(N). If E=E₃E₂E₁, direct expansion shows that E^{-1}L₃L₂L₁ is a product of one conjugate transposition for each odd layer, hence of at most two transpositions. Such an even residual is the identity, a 3-cycle, or two disjoint transpositions; the last case is a product of two 3-cycles. The sealed source supplies an arbitrary three-token cycle using a constant number of compound rotations, which becomes O(max{m,n})=O(N) bidirectional unit pushes. Thus every even permutation costs O(N). If a sortable permutation is odd, some dimension is even; one unit push on a line of that even length is odd, leaving an even residual. Therefore every sortable two-dimensional board is sortable in O(N) pushes.

The lower bound is also linear and explicit. A translation by floor(n/2) columns and floor(m/2) rows has exact distance m floor(n/2)+n floor(m/2). For m,n≥2 this is at least 2N/3. Hence D(m,n)=Θ(N) uniformly. If one dimension is one, the component consists only of N cyclic shifts and D=floor(N/2), so the asymptotic conclusion remains linear.

The audit's sole refutation is repaired: the reduced-word counting formula is stated only for m,n≥2. Its former one-dimensional wording was false because a 1×9 board has nine reachable states and diameter four, not a 9!/2-state component. All other audited progress is retained, including the FillColumns route, the corrected transpose dependencies, exact small diameters, and the displacement and counting analyses. Those earlier arguments supplied only Ω(N)≤D≤O(N log min{m,n}); the new layer decomposition supplies the missing O(N) construction. The requested target is therefore fully resolved.
